result.reason: No single killer found, but the opening is thin. Filing goes through the free national platform visitorlevy.scot. Booking tools already do the calculation and reporting: freeonlinebooking offers two levy reports you can email to the council, plus refunds and night caps. Hop and Bookster were also found earlier. I found no tool that submits returns to the platform, and no bulk upload or API. More councils are coming, which widens the market: Glasgow approved its levy with a start on 25 Jan 2027, and Stirling plans 2027. result.duty: Terrorism (Protection of Premises) Act 2025 (UK-wide). Standard tier (200-799 capacity; places of worship, childcare and education sites stay standard tier at any size): notify the SIA of the responsible person through an online portal the SIA is building, with volunteer testing from early 2027. Procedures for evacuation, invacuation, lockdown and communication must be in place so far as reasonably practicable. No physical works are required. The specific terrorism training requirement was dropped after consultation. Commencement is expected spring/April 2027, with the exact date to be confirmed by the SIA; final SIA guidance is due autumn 2026. Penalties for standard tier per secondary commentary (not confirmed on GOV.UK): up to GBP 10,000 fixed penalty plus GBP 500 per day. The duties carry on (inspections usually with 72 hours' notice), but notification looks one-off, and I found no mandated review or training frequency.
result.market: I found no official count of standard-tier premises; I did not reach the impact assessment. Pool Re estimates over 250,000 premises affected across all tiers. Places of worship come in at any capacity, but those normally under 200 people are generally out of scope. I did not verify how many village halls reach 200 capacity.
result.reason: The duty is real: the Terrorism (Protection of Premises) Act 2025 is UK law, and GOV.UK expects it to come into force in spring 2027. Responsible persons for premises holding 200 to 799 people must notify the SIA through a portal and put reasonably practicable procedures in place for evacuation, invacuation, lockdown and communication. Places of worship stay standard tier whatever their size. I found no dedicated tool for small venues: Hallmaster has none and teamSOS and Momentus aim elsewhere. But the free ProtectUK and Home Office guidance, insurer guides (Ecclesiastical, Methodist) and diocese and ACRE material cover most needs. The government dropped the standard template and the training requirement and says no paid services are needed. Notification looks one-off, so repeat demand is weak. Volunteer buyers will pay little.

result.competitor: None found for council licence application preparation or condition compliance. Clinic software such as Consentz, Pabau, Zenoti and Aesthetics Comply covers consent records, CQC compliance and general content, not the Scottish council licence. Councils' own forms and guidance and the Scottish Government's statutory guidance will be free. Law firms (Gilson Gray, MFMac) only offer commentary. result.duty: SSI 2026/87 (in force 13 Feb 2026) makes these procedures licensable under the Civic Government (Scotland) Act 1982 from 6 Sept 2027. They are chemical peels, cryolipolysis, cryotherapy, electrolysis, HIFU, microneedling, laser/light and RF. The council must inspect the premises before deciding. Before a licence is granted or renewed, the premises must have the listed facilities: a hands-free basin, sharps bin, autoclave or disposable instruments, and notices. Once licensed, the holder must meet ongoing conditions: single-use sterile needles, glove changes, sterilisation, waste arrangements, written aftercare information for clients, and no clients under 18. The licence names the practitioner, the premises and the business name. Applying before 6 Sept 2027 protects against prosecution while the application is pending (art. 6). Councils get 12 months to decide. Trading without a licence is an offence under s.7; the Order sets no penalty amounts. The Order sets no licence term, so it was not verified, and no fees were found. The separate Non-surgical Procedures and Functions of Medical Reviewers (Scotland) Act 2026 (asp 2026/13) restricts higher-risk procedures to HIS-regulated premises.
result.market: ONS Q1 2025 (cited in Business Gateway's May 2026 report): 3,940 hairdressing and beauty salons in Scotland, VAT/PAYE-registered only. Only a subset offer the licensable procedures, and unregistered sole traders and mobile or home practitioners are not counted. The Scottish Government's impact assessment (BRIA) says it has no hard data on sector size. Its business survey reached 665 recipients (591 responses), and 367 consultation respondents said they work in unregulated settings. A rough guess is 1,000–3,000 premises or practitioners affected; this is not verified.
result.reason: The duty is real. SSI 2026/87 has been in force since 13 Feb 2026. From 6 Sept 2027, providing listed procedures without a council licence is an offence under s.7 of the 1982 Act, unless an application was made before that date. A premises inspection is required before a decision. Conditions cover facilities, single-use needles, sterilisation, waste, aftercare information and no clients under 18. I found no Scotland-specific application or compliance tool or consultancy. Consentz, Pabau and Aesthetics Comply are aimed at CQC or consent records. The score is still low. Most demand is a one-off before Sept 2027. The application is a council form plus a physical facilities check. Renewals are infrequent (the licence term was not confirmed). Only a subset of about 3,940 salons offer these procedures, and buyers are price-sensitive.

result.competitor: Filing and payment go through the free state platform visitorlevy.scot, built by the Improvement Service. Booking and PMS tools found: Hop Software (calculates in night audit, Visitor Levy finance report), Bookster (levy uplift, return reporting 'to be reviewed' before October 2026), freetobook (shows the levy to guests only, no reports or filing), freeonlinebooking and Roommaster (guidance pages). No tool found that prepares the return or submits it to visitorlevy.scot. Airbnb tells Edinburgh hosts they must collect and remit the levy themselves. No bulk upload, agent access or API on the platform was confirmed. Eviivo, Guesty, Lodgify and Little Hotelier: not reached.
result.duty: Real and in force. Visitor Levy (Scotland) Act 2024, s.26: a return within 30 days of each period end, quarterly by default, with one assessment per premises. Penalties are in ss.47-50 and set by each council; further penalties can apply at 3, 6 and 12 months. Edinburgh's penalty framework (marked partly 'recommended, not implemented') gives a first penalty of 1% of rateable value (indicative £81 to £9,870) for non-residential premises and 10% of annual council tax for residential ones. The claimed 'GBP 100 plus 5%' penalty was not confirmed. Edinburgh: 5% of the accommodation charge for the first 5 nights, stays from 24 Jul 2026, bookings paid on or after 1 Oct 2025, 2% reimbursed to providers, records may be inspected. Glasgow: 5% from 25 Jan 2027. Aberdeen has approved 7% (start date not found). Stirling's earliest start is June 2027 and its final decision was not confirmed. Highland has paused its scheme.
result.market: Edinburgh had 3,209 short-term let licences in operation at 31 Dec 2025, and 32,317 across Scotland (Scottish Government statistics). Add Edinburgh B&Bs, guest houses and hotels; no count found. No published figure for providers registered on visitorlevy.scot was found. Glasgow joins in Jan 2027 and Aberdeen later, so roughly 4,000 to 6,000 liable small providers is plausible in the near term (an estimate).
result.reason: The duty is real. Under the Visitor Levy (Scotland) Act 2024, providers must make a return within 30 days of the end of each period, quarterly by default. Edinburgh's scheme is live: 5% for up to 5 nights, first return due October 2026, filed and paid on the free visitorlevy.scot platform. Glasgow starts 25 Jan 2027. Several booking systems (Hop, Bookster, freetobook, Roommaster) calculate the levy or offer reports, but none was found that files returns, and Bookster says its reporting is still under review. The gap is narrow: turning booking data into a per-property return. The buyers are small hosts with thin margins who get a 2% retention, so willingness to pay is limited. Bulk upload or API on the platform is unverified.

result.duty: Visitor Accommodation (Register and Levy) Etc. (Wales) Act 2025 (asc 2025/5), in force. result.duty: Heat network operators and suppliers in Great Britain (Ofgem authorisation regime, in force since 27 Jan 2026). Information required covers the organisation, ownership, financial resilience and consumer protection arrangements. Each operator must name a regulatory contact. Authorisation conditions and consumer standards apply now. From 27 Jan 2027, new networks must apply for authorisation before they start, then register within 3 months (interim arrangements under consultation until 2 Nov 2026). result.duty: Real and in force. Under the Deposit Scheme for Drinks Containers (England and Northern Ireland) Regulations 2025 (SI 2025/67, in force 24 Jan 2025), the deposit applies from 1 Oct 2027. Retailers may sell only registered and labelled products and must charge the 20p deposit. Grocery and convenience retailers must run a return point unless exempt, and all supermarkets and convenience stores selling in-scope drinks must register with EfC. Urban shops under 100 m2 are exempt automatically. Urban shops of 100-199 m2, rural shops under 200 m2, and shops with proximity, listed-building, access or utilities problems must apply (widened in June 2026). EfC registration Phase 1 is open with no formal deadline; Phase 2 is expected in Jan 2027. Return-handling fees were set in June 2026 and will be reviewed annually. Sources disagree on Wales: one says Wales withdrew, another says it plans its own scheme including glass from Oct 2027. I did not find the penalty provisions.

Duty is real: DAERA says professional users must keep PPP records (Reg 1107/2009 Art 67; enforced via PPP Regulations NI 2011, no penalty stated). Paper is accepted until 31 Dec 2026. Machine-readable electronic records are mandatory from 1 Jan 2027, with paper-created records converted by 31 Jan of the following year. However, DAERA already provides a free Excel spray-record template that meets Reg 2023/564, and farm management apps (e.g. Agroptima) exist. No submission portal found, so records are kept on request rather than filed. Market is small (NI farms and contractors, count not checked) and farmers are price-sensitive. The duty is real under the Veterinary Medicines Regulations 2013. GOV.UK criteria require records of receipt and supply of prescription medicines (date, product, batch, quantity, supplier or recipient, expiry, prescription details). Records are kept 5 years at the premises, may be electronic, and the retailer must do an annual stock audit. Penalties are weak. The duty is real, but it falls mainly on councils. The Private Water Supplies (England) Regulations 2016 require councils to risk assess every 5 years and to sample. Councils charge owners fees, and owners must keep the water wholesome and may be served notices. Councils say commercial supplies (including holiday lets and B&Bs) are sampled at least annually, though sources differ on once or twice a year. The owner has no filing duty beyond notifying the council and paying. DWI 2025 reports 34,102 private supplies in England serving 818k people; the commercial subset is not found. Competitor search was thin: I found no dedicated owner software, but I did not search vendors thoroughly. Pain is low, the buyer base is fragmented, and the workflow is thin (mostly UV maintenance logs). The 10 April 2026 DWI scheme update was not verified.

The England register is legislated (Levelling Up and Regeneration Act 2023) but not confirmed live. The gov.uk guidance says only that a digital development phase is under way. Frequency, fees, penalties and data fields are undecided. Reports give a March 2027 target (undated) and an earlier spring 2026 target that slipped. Claims of £2,500-£7,500 fines are unsourced. The filing route will be a free state online portal, with registration numbers shown on platform listings. This leaves little room for a paid third-party tool beyond safety-document reminders, and the existing vendors (Lodgify, Chekin, Goodlord) already publish guides. The host base is large, but many are hobbyists and most already use PMS or channel-manager tools. Frequency of the duty is unknown. Wales (31 March 2027 deadline) and Scotland already have schemes. I did not size the market from a register.

Duty is real in law but not yet operative. The Tobacco and Vapes Act 2026 (Royal Assent 29 Apr 2026) creates personal and premises licences for England, Wales and NI. No commencement date, fee, duration or application route is set. Poppleston Allen and Irwin Mitchell (31 Jul 2026) say the consultation has slipped to 2027. One council expects commencement Oct 2026 to Jan 2027, which conflicts with that. I found no licensing software; the only tools were product databases (Vapeclick) and an Australian POS. Competition is therefore open, but there is no workflow to build yet. Each council will run its own route, which fragments the market and makes it a one-off application rather than a recurring task. Scotland already has a free state register. I did not fetch pages or find retailer counts. Score stays at 3 and should be revisited once regulations are published.

The duty is real. Reg 40 (Children's Homes (England) Regs 2015, SI 2015/541) requires notifying Ofsted of serious events through an online form. Supported accommodation providers have a Reg 27 notification duty under SI 2023/416, in force since Oct 2023. Timing guidance conflicts, 24h in one source and 48h in another. I did not find or check any vendor, so competition is unverified, but care-management and children's home software is likely crowded (see K12). Weak points: the Ofsted form already handles the filing, notifications are event-driven and low volume, and many Reg 44 visitors use their own templates. Market is about 4,800 homes and 1,220 supported accommodation providers (claim figures, not re-verified). A small niche, so I give it a low score.
